steps.tx: Cardiac arrest is sudden loss of **effective mechanical blood flow** with pulselessness and apnoea, affecting about 10 per one hundred thousand people yearly. Survival to discharge is 10% in hospital and 5% out of hospital without CPR. Brain injury starts after 4 minutes without flow. High quality CPR chest depth is 5 to 6 cm at one hundred to one hundred twenty compressions per minute.
steps.say: Cardiac arrest stops blood flow with pulselessness and stopped breathing. Survival falls sharply without CPR. Brain injury starts after about four minutes without flow.

steps.tx: Common causes are **4 H and 4 T**: hypoxia, hypo or hyperkalaemia, hypothermia, acidosis, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins and thrombosis. Risk factors are ischaemic heart disease in 70%, age above 60, prior infarction and shock. Overdose with tricyclics causes 5% of in hospital arrests. K six point five mmol per L alone can cause bradycardic arrest.
steps.say: Causes follow the four H and four T pattern in resuscitation. Heart disease causes most arrests in adult patients. Low or high potassium can stop the heart quickly during arrest.

steps.tx: The **mechanism** begins when coronary flow falls below 15% of normal and myocardial ATP drops within 30 seconds. Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia cause 25% of arrests, while asystole and pulseless electrical activity cause 75%. Hypoxia raises acid load and drains glycogen in 10 minutes. Cerebral cortex loses eighty percent of ATP within 4 minutes.
steps.say: Coronary flow drops and heart muscle runs out of energy fast. Shockable rhythms cause about one quarter of arrests. Brain cells lose energy within four minutes.

steps.tx: Clinical features are unresponsiveness, absent pulse within 10 seconds, apnoea within 20 seconds and cyanosis in 2 minutes. **Classic sign** is agonal breaths that mimic normal breathing but signal arrest. Pupils dilate at 3 minutes and corneal reflex is lost at 10 minutes. Monitor shows VF, VT, asystole or pulseless electrical activity with organised complexes.
steps.say: The patient is unresponsive with no pulse and no breathing at all. Agonal breaths still indicate arrest and need immediate response. Pupils are dilated after about three minutes without flow.

steps.tx: First test is rhythm check on monitor with pulse check within 10 seconds, plus capnography showing ETCO2 below 10 mmHg. **Gold standard** is arterial line wave showing loss of pulsation and defibrillator rhythm analysis with pad placement. Arterial blood gas shows pH below seven point one and lactate above 10 mmol per L after 10 minutes. Echo excludes tamponade and pneumothorax in 5 minutes.
steps.say: Check pulse and rhythm in ten seconds for every arrest. Capnography falls below ten during arrest in most patients. Echo quickly checks for tamponade and tension pneumothorax.

steps.tx: First line is high quality CPR with **adrenaline** 1 mg every 3 to 5 minutes plus amiodarone 300 mg then 150 mg for shockable rhythms. Use biphasic energy one hundred twenty to two hundred J for VF and VT. Give oxygen 15 litres per min and secure airway within 10 minutes. Push hard and fast with depth 5 to 6 cm and full recoil one hundred to one hundred twenty per minute.
steps.say: Adrenaline one milligram every three to five minutes is the backbone. Amiodarone follows for shockable rhythms. Compressions must be deep and fast with full recoil.

steps.tx: After ROSC, target MAP sixty-five to eighty mmHg, SpO2 94 to 98% and temperature control at 36 degrees for 24 hours. Use anticoagulant eighty units per kg bolus then 18 units per kg per hour for STEMI with **antiplatelet agent** 180 mg load. Correct K to 4 to 5 mmol per L and Mg above 2 mg per dL. Start dual antiplatelet within 24 hours when coronary cause is proven.
steps.say: After return of circulation, keep pressure and oxygen in a safe range. Cooling to thirty six degrees protects the brain. Heart block and potassium must be corrected.

steps.tx: Shockable versus non shockable arrest needs different drug order in the first 10 minutes. **Comparison** shows survival 30% with VF defibrillated within 3 minutes versus 5% after 10 minutes. Amiodarone raises ROSC by 15% in shock refractory VF. Adrenaline every 5 minutes raises survival but with 10% worse neurology when given late.
steps.say: Shockable rhythms need defibrillation within three minutes for best survival. Amiodarone helps refractory VF in the unit at once. Adrenaline timing affects brain recovery after arrest a lot.

steps.tx: Complications include **rib fractures** in 30%, sternal injury in 15%, aspiration in 20% and ICU myopathy in 25%. Neurological injury affects 50% of survivors with hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy. Recurrent arrest occurs in 40% within 24 hours. Prognosis is best with bystander CPR within 4 minutes, raising good neurology to 40% from 5%.
steps.say: Rib fractures occur in about thirty percent of CPR. Brain injury affects half of survivors. Physical injury is common but recovery is possible with fast CPR.

steps.tx: Prognosis predictors are **witnessed arrest**, bystander CPR within 4 minutes, VF as first rhythm and ROSC within 20 minutes. ETCO2 above 20 mmHg during CPR predicts ROSC in eighty percent. Pupils equal and reactive at 24 hours predict good outcome with 90% accuracy. Survivors need ICU care for 3 to 5 days and echo within 12 hours.
steps.say: Witnessed arrest with fast bystander CPR gives the best odds. Pupil signs reflect recovery well after arrest. ICU care for three to five days is standard care.

steps.tx: **High-yield for the exam** table for cardiac arrest and resuscitation in seven high yield points. Remember CPR depth 5 to 6 cm, rate one hundred to one hundred twenty per minute, adrenaline 1 mg every 3 to 5 minutes and biphasic two hundred J. Shockable rhythms are 25% and non shockable 75%. Brain injury begins after 4 minutes without flow.
steps.say: This table has the numbers to quote quickly. Rate depth drugs and energy are the core facts.
